newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries end lower as Greenspan awaited Thur.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries end lower as Greenspan awaited Thur.

text.p: U.S. government securities prices closed lower Wednesday as Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's scheduled testimony on the economy on Thursday took center stage on players' minds.

Greenspan will testify before the Congressional Joint Economic Committee Thursday at 1000 EST/1500 GMT on monetary policy, interest rates and other topics. It will his last publicly scheduled appearance before next week's policy-making Federal Open Market Committee meeting. While not expected to tip the FOMC's hand, his comments will be scrutinized closely.
On Wednesday overnight gains were erased by a slightly stronger than expected consumer price index (up 0.3 percent) early in the session and a negative tone persisted throughout the session.

"The bond market's performance today, at least indirectly, can be tied to CPI. It was a reasonably good report -- a bit firmer than expected -- but it showed inflation stable," said Michael Moran, chief economist at Daiwa Securities America Inc. "The problem was it wasn't so favorable that it would rule out a tightening by the Fed, so we some deterioration in prices as this realization started to sink in."
Moran said Greenspan's testimony on Thursday would likely be similar to what he said at the Humphrey-Hawkins hearings.

"He'll acknowledge that the economy is performing well, but that does not answer the question of whether they tighten at the next meeting," Moran said. As a result, bond prices probably would be little changed but with a negative bias, he said.

Yields on the 30-year bond touched upon the 7.0 percent level several times during Wednesday's trading session but couldn't gather the downward momentum necessary to breach the psychologically important mark.

Matt Alexy, chief market strategist at Credit Suisse First Boston, there was definitely near-term support for yields at current levels of about 7.0 percent on the bond and 6-3/4 percent on the 10-year.
No one, however, was defending the levels in a big way with the memory of a buyer a couple of days ago still fresh.

"We have Greenspan tomorrow and the FOMC next week. Few participants are going to make big stands until after the meeting," Alexy said. Players wanted time to guage the strength of the economy regardless of what the Fed did, he said, and little meaningful movement was seen until they did.

"We may be entering a period where interest rates are expected to be higher, but we're not going to be seeing the federal funds rate doubling," Alexy said. Without obvious inflationary pressure the Fed could tinker rather than have to recast the economy.
Such sentiment has led many economists to expect the Fed to tighten only once before returning to a neutral stance and perhaps even easing later in the year.
They argue the Fed only needs to slow the overheated pace of growth seen in the fourth quarter of last year, a pace seemingly continuing into the first quarter of 1997.
The Treasury's 30-year bond ended 10/32 lower at 95-15/32 to yield 6.99 percent.
Three-month bills closed up one basis point at 5.15 percent; six-month bills were up two basis points at 5.29 percent and year-bill rates ended two basis points higher at 5.46 percent.
Two-year notes ended down 1/32 at 99-12/32, yielding 6.22 percent. Five-year notes closed down 3/32 at 98-20/32, yielding 6.58 percent. Ten-year notes fell 4/32 to 96-16/32, yielding 6.74 percent.
